extracted.intended_audience: students and competitors solving classical Euclidean geometry problems (advanced high-school / early undergraduate)
extracted.subtask_description: Solution techniques, lemmas and constructive methods for classical Euclidean-geometry contest problems (congruence, cyclic quadrilaterals, tetrahedra, projections, inequalities, spherical geometry, constructions). Targets producing correct geometric constructions and inequalities and recognizing equality cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of skew quadrilaterals with congruent opposite sides
rubrics_metrics.description: If opposite sides of a skew quadrilateral ABCD are congruent then ABC ∼ ACD and ABD ∼ BCD; with P,Q midpoints of AC and BD we have |PD| = |PB| ⇒ PQ ⟂ BD and |PA| = |PC| ⇒ PQ ⟂ AC. Conversely, if PQ ⟂ AC and PQ ⟂ BD then a half turn about PQ switches A↔C and B↔D, so opposite sides are congruent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use midpoint and perpendicular-bisector arguments and the half-turn (180° rotation) symmetry about the line PQ to characterize congruence of opposite sides in skew quadrilaterals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Ptolemy's theorem to derive length inequalities in cyclic quadrilaterals
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying Ptolemy to appropriate cyclic quadrilaterals yields inequalities such as |AA1| > (|AB| + |AC|)/2 and analogous results for related vertices; summing yields |AA1| + |BB1| + |CC1| > |AB| + |BC| + |CA|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify cyclic 4-tuples and apply Ptolemy's relation |AC|·|BB1| ≤ |AB|·|CB1| + |CB|·|AB1|, use symmetry of equal subtended arcs and triangle inequalities (e.g., |A1B| + |A1C| > |BC|) to obtain the desired bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equilateral triangle result when angles are 120°
rubrics_metrics.description: If the relevant angles are each 120°, then a constructed triangle PQR (in the given configuration) is equilateral; consequently the differences of opposite sides are equal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize 120° angle configurations simplify to equilateral or symmetric substructures; exploit equal angles to deduce side equalities or constant differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maximizing chord length via diameter choice (constant subtended angle)
rubrics_metrics.description: For a point P moving on a circle Z with diameter AP, the subtended angle MAN remains constant; |MN| is maximal when AP is a diameter, in which case M,N coincide with fixed vertices (B,C) and |MN|max = |BC|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the property 'angle in a semicircle is right' and that a fixed subtended angle corresponds to a fixed chord length; maximize the diameter AP to maximize the chord MN.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perimeter comparison of inscribed triangles using sine law and monotonicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Among triangles inscribed in the same circle with the same base, the triangle with larger altitude has larger perimeter; via a = 2r sin α the sum a + b = 2r(sin α + sin β) is a decreasing function of |α − β|, so minimizing |α − β| maximizes a + b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the Sine Law, transform sums using trig identities (sum-to-product), and use monotonicity/Jordan's inequality (sin x > 2x/π on (0,π/2)) to obtain succinct lower bounds (e.g., a+b+c > 4r).

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative perpendicular-chord construction to obtain product property
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct a chain of perpendiculars P P1 ⟂ A1A2, P P2 ⟂ A2A3, ... with Pk ∈ A{k−1}A{k}, and then show the product P1P2·...·Pn has the required property (as in problem statement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use inductive / iterative construction of perpendicular segments at successive sides/edges; exploit similarity and repeated perpendicular relationships to establish multiplicative relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closing an open chain of chords by adjusting circle radius and center
rubrics_metrics.description: Place the longest side as a chord in a large circle, place other chords arbitrarily to form an open chain, then continuously decrease the radius until the chain closes; if it closes with the midpoint on the other side, adjust radius again to obtain closure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use continuity of chord endpoints with respect to circle radius/center and intermediate value-type reasoning to show existence of a radius producing a closed polygonal chain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intersection of bisecting planes yields insphere center
rubrics_metrics.description: The three bisecting planes of a solid angle intersect in a line which is the locus equidistant from the faces; intersecting with another bisecting plane produces O equidistant from all four faces, i.e., the center of the inscribed sphere of a tetrahedron.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit the definition of bisecting planes (points equidistant from two faces) and intersect them to find a unique point equidistant from all faces (insphere center).

rubrics_metrics.name: Property of a solid-angle bisector: equidistance from faces
rubrics_metrics.description: Any point on the bisector of a solid angle is equidistant from the faces of that solid angle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use perpendicular distances to planes (faces) to characterize points on the bisector; this is used to deduce symmetry/center relations in 3D solids.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing regular space polygons from plane polygons by bending/lifting
rubrics_metrics.description: For n≥4 (various constructions given per parity), start from a plane polygon (rhombus, regular n-gon, strip of squares), then bend or lift alternate vertices by appropriate amounts to obtain a regular space polygon with specified equal angles (including α = 90° cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perform local foldings or vertical displacements of selected vertices (every second vertex) preserving edge lengths to produce nonplanar regular polygons; explicit constructions given for even/odd n and special α.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section parallel to an edge intersects at least four vertices
rubrics_metrics.description: Take a section parallel to an edge e that intersects all edges ending in e; because at least two other edges end at each endpoint of e, the intersection section has at least four vertices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use combinatorial adjacency at endpoints of an edge and planarity of section to lower-bound the number of intersection vertices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bounding total edge length via orthogonal projections
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct planes perpendicular to AB through each vertex and note that the orthogonal projection of the polyhedron's edge network onto AB covers AB at least three times; consequently the sum of edge lengths is greater than 3·d (distance between two farthest vertices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare lengths with projections onto a fixed line: each nonparallel segment contributes at least its projected length; counting multiplicity of coverage gives a global lower bound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spherical reflection to locate points inside spherical triangles
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflect the spherical triangle ABC in the center O to get A'B'C'; then the reflected point D' must lie inside A'B'C' (used to deduce location of original D).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use central symmetry (antipodal reflection) on the sphere to transfer inclusion relations between spherical triangles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upper bound on number of acute angles in an n-gon via angle-sum accounting
rubrics_metrics.description: Let k be the number of acute angles in an n-gon; equate total angle sum two ways (k·90°+(n−k)·360° = (n−2)·180°) to deduce 3k > 2n+4 and hence k ≤ [2n/3] +1. Constructions show this bound is sharp for n ≡ 0,1,2 (mod 3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count angles by type and manipulate linear inequalities; provide concrete constructions to achieve equality cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three pairwise-intersecting circles lying on spheres must have a common point
rubrics_metrics.description: If circle1 and circle2 lie on sphere s1, and circle2 and circle3 on s2, and s1 ≠ s2, then their spheres' intersection line is circle2; the common point of circle1 and circle3 also lies on that line, so all three circles share a point — contradiction if assumed otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lift planar circle configurations to spheres (take circles as intersections of spheres with a plane) and reason about sphere intersections (lines) to show forced common points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complete-graph-on-vertices implies triangular faces (convex polyhedron)
rubrics_metrics.description: If every vertex of a (convex) polyhedron is joined by edges to every other vertex, then all faces must be triangular (otherwise cutting along certain edges would separate the surface incorrectly).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use adjacency and convexity: presence of a face with >3 vertices contradicts the ability to join all vertices by edges without intersections; nonconvex counterexamples exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinatorial divisibility constraints on faces and edges
rubrics_metrics.description: If a convex polyhedron has only triangular faces and f faces then number of edges is 3f/2 (thus divisible by 3). If any face has more than three edges, the number of edges is at least eight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Count incidences of edges per face and use handshaking/counting arguments to derive divisibility and bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of spheres with given circles as equators to show common point above plane
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct spheres that have the given planar circles as equators; by analyzing diameters of their pairwise intersection circles (one diameter inside third sphere, one outside), conclude the third sphere intersects the circle and hence the three spheres share a point above the plane.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate planar circle intersection problems into 3D sphere intersection geometry, and use relative positions of diameters to force intersection points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projection argument with parallelogram to guarantee projection ratio ≥ √2
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a parallelogram with sides a ≤ b and diagonal d, the projection onto a line ⟂ b is ≤ a while projection onto a line parallel to d equals d; using d² > a² + b² ≥ 2a² gives a projection ratio ≥ √2 (so two planes perpendicular to a given plane exist with projection ratio ≥ √2).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose projection directions strategically (perpendicular to one side and parallel to diagonal) and use diagonal-length inequalities to bound ratios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Counting noncoplanar quadruples by complementary pairing (box counting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Among the 70 choices of 4 vertices from 8, 12 are coplanar leaving 58 noncoplanar quadruples which form 29 complementary pairs; each complementary pair determines the same box, hence there are 29 boxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use combinatorial selection, remove coplanar subsets, then identify complementary pairings that produce identical geometric objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivation of Erdős–Mordell inequality via perpendiculars and area relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Drop perpendiculars from A and B to CP and use relations between distances to sides and triangle area to obtain inequalities cz ≥ au + bv etc.; combining and symmetrizing yields x + y + z ≥ 2(u + v + w), the Erdős–Mordell inequality, with equality for the equilateral triangle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce perpendicular distances from an interior point to sides, relate them to areas and side lengths, use reflections across angle bisectors to permute variables and sum inequalities to obtain the classical bound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Angle-sum and area algebra to deduce β + δ ≥ π in a quadrilateral
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a + c = b + d and area A = √(abcd), express AC² two ways (cos law), equate area formulae ab/2 sin β + cd/2 sin δ = √(abcd), manipulate to derive cos(β + δ) ≤ −1 which implies β + δ ≥ π.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine side-sum condition with law of cosines and area expressions; multiply and expand carefully to force a bound on cosine of angle sum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of quadratic/root multiplicity to deduce ordering of triangle sides
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a ≤ b ≤ c ≤ k with f(x)=x+2A/x, if f(a)=f(b)=f(c)=k then the quadratic equation f(x)=k has at most two distinct solutions so at least two sides coincide, leading to ordering constraints a ≤ b ≤ c.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate geometric inequalities to algebraic constraints (quadratic equation) and use root multiplicity limits to deduce equalities/ordering among side lengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closure of equal-step circular sequence iff rotation angle rational multiple of π
rubrics_metrics.description: A sequence of points obtained by reflecting/jumping at fixed angle α closes (finite cycle) iff α is a rational multiple of π (α = p/q·π), because the points map to equally spaced arcs on a circle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model the jump/reflection sequence as an arc-translation on a circle; closure corresponds to finite-order rotation in the circle group (rational angle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Covering sphere by spherical caps placed at cube vertices
rubrics_metrics.description: To cover the sphere with caps of angular radius φ satisfying cos φ = 1/3, place eight caps with centers at vertices of an inscribed cube; the angular distance between neighboring vertices also satisfies cos φ1 = 1/3, so every point is covered at least twice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute angular distances using the space diagonal relation (d=√3 a) and the Cosine Rule; choose symmetric polyhedron (cube) vertices to optimize uniform coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Similarity of triangles formed by differences of opposite sides in hexagon
rubrics_metrics.description: In a hexagon with parallels drawn through certain vertices, the triangle PQR formed from differences of opposite sides is similar to the triangle STU obtained from the other alternating triple because their sides equal differences of opposite sides (e.g., |PQ| = |AB − DE| etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate side differences to side-lengths of constructed triangles and use similarity to compare areas or other measures (e.g., area(ACE) expressed via ABCDEF and PQR).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute circumcircle radius for arc one-third of circle (120° central angle)
rubrics_metrics.description: If arc ACB is one-third of the circle then angle AMB = 120° at the center; with side lengths a = |BC|, b = |AC|, c = |AB| one has c² = a² + b² + ab and the radius r satisfies r = sqrt((a² + b² + ab)/3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the law of cosines to triangle with central angle 120° and convert to radius via standard relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Searchlight–boat pursuit: use path-length and speed ratio inequalities for feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Model the searchlight's illuminated path length on the unit circle and compare with boat's covered distance given speed ratio s/b; derive inequalities (e.g., k < 2π + 1 or critical k ≈ 7.789705781) that determine whether the boat can be found/escape.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute angular distances and corresponding arc lengths for the searchlight, compute boat travel distances in same time intervals, and compare to obtain threshold conditions on k = s/b.

rubrics_metrics.name: Volume proportionality of pyramids to altitudes and AM–HM bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Volumes of pyramids with same base are proportional to altitudes; combining such decompositions for a tetrahedron yields relations among distances from vertices to opposite faces, and applying AM–HM inequalities gives lower bounds on sums of these distances in terms of the insphere radius R.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use additive decomposition of tetrahedron volume into pyramids over faces, express in terms of face areas and altitudes, then apply classical inequalities (AM–HM) to obtain numeric bounds and equality conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symmetric minimization: equality occurs when variables equal (insphere midpoint minimizer)
rubrics_metrics.description: For minimization problems of symmetric form (e.g., minimize Σ Si/xi subject to constraints), equality / minimizer occurs when x1 = x2 = x3 = x4 = r (radius of inscribed sphere); the midpoint of the inscribed sphere minimizes Σ Si/xi.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit symmetry and use AM-GM or related inequalities; check equality condition to identify geometric minimizer (center of insphere).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lagrange/complete-square method for minimizing sum of squared distances to triangle sides
rubrics_metrics.description: Minimize x² + y² + z² subject to ax + by + cz = constant by completing the square: (x−λa)² + (y−λb)² + (z−λc)² − λ²(a²+b²+c²). Minimum occurs when x:y:z = a:b:c; the minimizing point is the Lemoine point (symmedian intersection) with explicit coordinates x = (2Δ a)/(a²+b²+c²), etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Lagrange multipliers or complete-the-square technique; identify the geometric point (Lemoine) that realizes the minimum and compute the minimal value algebraically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tangents-from-point perimeter decomposition implies sum of inradii equality
rubrics_metrics.description: For a triangle with incircle and three tangent subtriangles, perimeters satisfy p1 + p2 + p3 = p; since pi = π·ri and p = π·r, one gets r1 + r2 + r3 = r.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use equal tangent-length property and relation between perimeter and inradius for triangles to deduce additive relations among inradii.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sum of radii of inscribed spheres for tetrahedron subdivisions equals twice insphere radius
rubrics_metrics.description: Suppose Fi, hi, ri are face areas, altitudes and radii of the four small inspheres in a tetrahedron with insphere radius r; algebraic relations among Fi, hi, ri yield r1 + r2 + r3 + r4 = 2r.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use similarity relations between small inscribed spheres and whole tetrahedron, express volumes and altitudes, and equate to derive sum relations for radii.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimal-area isosceles triangle cut from an angle (angle bisector condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given angle α ≥ 60° and bisector AD > 1, among lines through D cutting from α a triangle of minimal area, the minimal triangle is isosceles and its area exceeds 1/√3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Optimize area under length constraints by symmetry: the minimum is achieved when the cut produces an isosceles triangle; compute numeric lower bound by analyzing geometry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Midpoints of opposite edges of tetrahedra from skew cube edges coincide at cube center
rubrics_metrics.description: Take three skew edges of a cube (each edge being part of one tetrahedron); the midpoints of opposite edges of each tetrahedron coincide at the cube center, and the three tetrahedra have no additional common points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use midpoint symmetry and spatial reasoning in cube; check intersection structure to verify only the center is shared among midpoints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of cyclicity and trapezoid similarity to relate segment sums
rubrics_metrics.description: From similar triangles (e.g., O1BE ∼ O2BF) deduce that points E,F,O1,O2 lie on a circle C; further similarity leads to equilateral trapezoids and equalities like AE + AF = MB + BN = MN.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit inscribed angle equalities, cyclic quadrilaterals and trapezoid similarity to convert angular relations to linear equalities of segment sums.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Ceva and projection ratios to derive triangle similarities
rubrics_metrics.description: Project vertices onto a line B1C1 to points D,P,K; using Ceva’s theorem and proportionality of segments deduce triangles PMB and KMC are similar (PM/CK = (BC1/C1A)·(AB1/B1C) = BA1/A1C etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine projective ratios from Ceva with elementary similarity rules to transform projection relations into triangle similarity conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ptolemy bounds for distances from an external point to square vertices
rubrics_metrics.description: For point M with MA + MB = a (A,B adjacent vertices of square ABCD), use Ptolemy on quadrilateral AMBC to derive bounds like MC ≤ (MA + MB)/√(2+1?) and similarly for MD; adding yields MC + MD ≤ sqrt((MA + MB)(...)) with equality when M is on circumcircle of square.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Ptolemy inequality to appropriate quadrilaterals involving the point and square to bound sums of distances to other vertices; interpret equality geometrically (circumcircle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-color triangulation argument to deduce divisibility properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Color the triangulation of an n-gon by two colors alternating when adding diagonals; the count of white triangle sides w is a multiple of 3, and since black sides b = n + w and 3 divides both n+w and w, 3 divides n.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use an inductive coloring rule when drawing diagonals and count side incidences across colors; parity/triangular-count constraints produce divisibility conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct arrow orientation on diagonals/sides to obtain zero vector sum by rotational symmetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Orient sides and main diagonals so their vector sum is zero by placing arrows cyclically (odd n) or organizing cycles of main diagonals and remaining sides (even n) exploiting invariance under rotations by 2π/(2k+1) or π/k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit rotational symmetry of a regular n-gon to assign vector directions in invariant patterns yielding net zero sum; handle odd and even n separately.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perpendicularity via inscribed-angle equalities yielding orthocenter membership
rubrics_metrics.description: Construct K = AN∩BD and L = BD∩AM; using inscribed-angle equalities (e.g., LAN = NDL = 45°) show quadrilaterals are cyclic and AL ⟂ LN, MK ⟂ AN, so MK and NL are altitudes of triangle AMN and intersect at orthocenter H; thus AH is the third altitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use angle-chasing and cyclic quadrilateral detection to identify right angles and conclude orthocenter / altitude relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parallelogram/square detection from angle equalities and symmetries
rubrics_metrics.description: From equal angle sums and pairwise equal segments (O4O1 ∼ O2O3 etc.) deduce O1O2O3O4 is a parallelogram with congruent opposite angles; additional symmetry (O4O2 as symmetry line) implies it is a square.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate angle equalities into side/parallel relations, identify symmetry lines to upgrade parallelogram to rectangle/square.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proving perpendicularity by chain of similar triangles and ratio equalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish KP/PL = BE/CF and related equal ratios via triangle similarities (BP K ∼ DBE, etc.), derive MQ/QN equalities, and combining KP/PL = MQ/QN conclude PL = QN and thus PQ ⟂ AD because KP + PL over PL equals MQ + QN over QN.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: String together several similarity relations to equate segment ratios; transform ratio equalities into equalities of sums that imply perpendicularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructing a great circle through three points on a sphere via planar circumcircle
rubrics_metrics.description: Given three points A,B,C on a sphere, construct triangle A'B'C' similar in a plane and its circumcircle center O'; construct right triangles and perpendiculars (using projection from sphere center) to locate the great circle center/diameter on the sphere and thereby the circle through A,B,C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduce the spherical construction to a planar circumcircle problem by projecting to a suitable plane, then lift back using right-triangle constructions to find the great circle on the sphere.
